vf[0]: The monitor shows **ventricular fibrillation (VF)**: a shockable rhythm. What first?
[RIGHT] Shock now (defibrillate), then straight back to CPR -> VF or pulseless VT is shockable: shock as soon as the pads are on, then straight back to 2 minutes of CPR.
Epinephrine 1 mg IV first, then shock at the next rhythm check -> In VF the shock comes first. Epinephrine goes in after the second shock.
Stop CPR and feel for a pulse for a full minute first -> A pulse check takes under 10 seconds. Every pause stops blood flow to the brain.
Synchronized cardioversion at 100 J, then CPR -> Synchronized cardioversion needs a QRS to time the shock to. VF has none: defibrillate (an unsynchronized shock).
vf[1]: Two minutes of CPR. Rhythm check: **still VF**.
[RIGHT] Shock again, then epinephrine 1 mg IV every 3 to 5 minutes -> Still shockable: shock every time, then epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes.
Amiodarone 300 mg instead of a second shock, then recheck -> Shock every time the rhythm is shockable. Drugs support the shocks; they don't replace them.
Hold CPR, intubate first, then shock once the tube is secure -> Keep compressions going. A bag-mask works; a tube can go in without stopping CPR.
Sodium bicarbonate 50 mEq, as in every arrest, then shock -> Bicarbonate is for specific causes (high potassium, some overdoses), not every arrest.
vf[2]: Two more minutes. **Still VF** after two shocks and epinephrine.
[RIGHT] Shock, then amiodarone 300 mg IV -> VF that won't stop after shocks: amiodarone (lidocaine is the other choice). Keep shocking every 2 minutes.
Adenosine 6 mg rapid push, then recheck -> Adenosine is for SVT in a patient with a pulse.
Call the code: it has been 4 minutes already -> Far too early to stop. VF is the rhythm most likely to come back.
Atropine 1 mg IV, then shock at the next check -> Atropine is for a slow heart with a pulse. It was taken out of the cardiac arrest algorithm in 2010.
pea[0]: The monitor shows **a rhythm but no pulse (PEA)**: not shockable. What first?
[RIGHT] Keep CPR going; epinephrine 1 mg IV now -> Not shockable: CPR, and epinephrine as soon as possible, then every 3 to 5 minutes.
Shock it at 200 J, then resume CPR -> PEA and asystole are not shockable. A shock only pauses CPR. (A flat line: check the leads and the gain first.)
Atropine 1 mg IV, repeated every 3 minutes -> Atropine is for a slow heart with a pulse. It was taken out of the cardiac arrest algorithm in 2010.
Wait for respiratory therapy before compressions -> Compressions start now, with whoever is in the room.
pea[1]: Two minutes later, **still no pulse**. What are you hunting for?

[RIGHT] The reversible causes: the H's and T's -> Not shockable: the way back is the cause. Hunt the H's and T's: low volume, low oxygen, acid, potassium, cold, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, clot.
Nothing new: keep repeating epinephrine on time -> Repeating epinephrine without looking for the cause rarely ends well.
A shock every 2 minutes in case it turns to VF -> Only shock a shockable rhythm. Check it every 2 minutes.
Amiodarone 300 mg, then recheck -> Amiodarone is for VF and pulseless VT, not PEA or asystole.

trauma[0]: A traumatic arrest: **no pulse, PEA** on the monitor. What first?

[RIGHT] Blood, bleeding control, airway, and both sides of the chest decompressed, all at once -> A traumatic arrest is fixed by its causes, all at once: stop the bleeding, give blood, secure the airway, decompress both sides of the chest. Epinephrine and CPR do little without volume.
Epinephrine 1 mg every 3 minutes and good CPR, nothing else yet -> In a traumatic arrest, drugs alone don't replace lost blood.
Shock it at 200 J, then 2 minutes of CPR and epinephrine -> PEA and asystole are not shockable. A shock only pauses CPR. (A flat line: check the leads and the gain first.)
Normal saline, six liters as fast as it will run, then reassess them -> Blood, not liters of saline: saline thins what is left.
trauma[1]: Blood is going in and both sides of the chest are decompressed. The ultrasound shows **fluid around the heart**.
[RIGHT] Drain it now (pericardiocentesis), or the surgeon opens the chest -> Fluid around the heart squeezing it: drain it now (pericardiocentesis), or the surgeon opens the chest.
Amiodarone 300 mg IV, then shock if the rhythm changes -> Amiodarone is for VF and pulseless VT, not PEA or asystole.
Synchronized cardioversion at 100 J to restart the heart -> Synchronized cardioversion needs a QRS to time the shock to. VF has none: defibrillate (an unsynchronized shock).
Sodium bicarbonate and calcium, as in every arrest, then recheck -> Bicarbonate is for specific causes (high potassium, some overdoses), not every arrest.

cause:k: [RIGHT] Calcium chloride and sodium bicarbonate; keep CPR going -> High potassium in arrest: calcium to protect the heart and sodium bicarbonate are the usual first moves (the evidence is thin), with insulin and dextrose as a bolus, and dialysis.
Start an insulin drip and recheck the potassium in an hour -> A drip and an hour is too slow. In arrest: calcium first, insulin with dextrose as a bolus, and call for dialysis.
Shock it at 200 J, then 2 minutes of CPR -> PEA and asystole are not shockable. A shock only pauses CPR. (A flat line: check the leads and the gain first.)

cause:trap: Severe asthma: the chest is **stiff and over-full**, and each breath gets harder.

[RIGHT] Pause the bag, press the chest to let air out, slow the breaths -> In an asthma arrest, air gets trapped: breathe slowly, let it out (disconnect, press on the chest), and think of a tension pneumothorax on either side.
Bag faster and harder to push more oxygen past the tight airways -> Faster, harder breaths trap more air and drop the pressure further.
A double dose of epinephrine, then keep bagging hard -> A bigger dose of epinephrine doesn't help. Fix the airway.
Shock it at 200 J, then 2 minutes of CPR and recheck -> PEA and asystole are not shockable. A shock only pauses CPR. (A flat line: check the leads and the gain first.)
cause:air: The bag-mask **isn't moving the chest** well.
[RIGHT] Reposition, two-person bag-mask, then a tube, without stopping CPR -> Fix the airway: reposition, a two-person bag-mask, then an advanced airway, all without stopping compressions.
Stop CPR until the breathing tube is in, then restart compressions -> Stopping compressions to place a tube costs more than it gains.
A double dose of epinephrine to open up the airways -> A bigger dose of epinephrine doesn't help. Fix the airway.
More sodium bicarbonate to correct the acid from poor breathing -> Bicarbonate is for specific causes (high potassium, some overdoses), not every arrest.

[RIGHT] Massive transfusion, and a surgeon or IR to stop the bleeding -> A bleed inside the body: blood (massive transfusion) and a surgeon or interventional radiology to stop it. CPR can't fill an empty heart.
Tenecteplase, in case a clot is behind this arrest -> A clot buster in a bleeding patient makes it worse.
Shock it at 200 J, then 2 minutes of CPR and epinephrine -> PEA and asystole are not shockable. A shock only pauses CPR. (A flat line: check the leads and the gain first.)
Nothing changes: epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes and wait for labs -> Repeating epinephrine without looking for the cause rarely ends well.

[RIGHT] Fluids wide open, while CPR and epinephrine go on -> An empty heart: fluids wide open, while CPR and epinephrine go on.
Tenecteplase, in case a clot is behind this arrest -> An empty heart needs volume, not a clot buster: nothing here points to a clot, and the drug risks bleeding.
Shock it at 200 J, then 2 minutes of CPR -> PEA and asystole are not shockable. A shock only pauses CPR. (A flat line: check the leads and the gain first.)
Nothing changes: epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes -> Repeating epinephrine without looking for the cause rarely ends well.
cause:opioid: They were found **not breathing**, pupils pinpoint.
[RIGHT] Oxygen and ventilation; naloxone is reasonable; CPR goes on -> An opioid arrest is a breathing arrest: oxygen and good ventilation first. Naloxone is reasonable, but it never replaces CPR.
Give naloxone and stop CPR until it starts working -> Never stop CPR to wait for naloxone.
Flumazenil, to reverse whatever they took, then recheck -> Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids, and can cause seizures.
Shock it at 200 J, then 2 minutes of CPR and more epinephrine -> PEA and asystole are not shockable. A shock only pauses CPR. (A flat line: check the leads and the gain first.)
cause:tension: No breath sounds on one side, and the **trachea is pushed to the other side**.
[RIGHT] Decompress that side now, with a needle or a finger -> No breath sounds and a shifted trachea: a tension pneumothorax. Decompress now; don't wait for an X-ray.
A portable chest X-ray first, to be sure which side it is -> A tension pneumothorax is a clinical call. There is no time for an X-ray in arrest.
A double dose of epinephrine, then keep bagging -> A bigger dose of epinephrine doesn't help. Fix the airway.
Shock it at 200 J, then 2 minutes of CPR and recheck -> PEA and asystole are not shockable. A shock only pauses CPR. (A flat line: check the leads and the gain first.)
cause:clot: The ultrasound shows **a huge right heart** and a clot in the leg.
[RIGHT] Tenecteplase (a clot buster) during CPR, and keep going -> A big clot in the lungs causing the arrest: a clot buster (tenecteplase) during CPR is reasonable, and CPR goes on longer after it.
Stop now: an arrest from a clot this size can't come back -> A PE arrest can come back, especially with a clot buster.
Heparin drip, and recheck the rhythm and pulse in an hour -> Heparin stops new clot; it won't break this one in time.
Shock it at 200 J, then 2 minutes of CPR and recheck -> PEA and asystole are not shockable. A shock only pauses CPR. (A flat line: check the leads and the gain first.)

Stop: an arrest from a heart attack can't come back, so call it -> Arrests from a heart attack often come back, and the cath lab can fix the cause.
